opus-5.5.text:
I think "world model" has become one of those terms where everyone uses the same words but means slightly different things, so it helps to separate a few layers.

The most classical meaning comes from reinforcement learning and control. A world model is something that, given the current state and an action, predicts what happens next: the next state, maybe the reward. If you have that, you can plan inside your head instead of trying everything in the real world. That's the narrow, technical definition, and it's very clean.

Then there's a second usage that has become popular with video generation. People say a model that generates realistic, physically consistent video is a "world model" because it seems to have internalized how objects move, how light works, how things collide. That's related, but I'd be a bit careful. Generating pixels that look right is not the same as having a representation you can query, intervene on, and use for decisions. Something can be a very good renderer without being a very good simulator for planning.

The third usage is the broadest, and honestly the one I find most interesting: the idea that a large language model, by predicting text, ends up building some internal model of the world. Text is a compressed record of how humans describe reality, including causes, intentions, and consequences. To predict it well you have to model a lot of the underlying structure. In that sense, LLMs already have a kind of world model, just not a perceptual or physical one. It's more abstract, more about concepts and agents than about pixels and trajectories.

So when I hear researchers argue about whether models "have a world model," I usually ask: a model of which world, at what level of abstraction, and for what purpose? If the purpose is acting, whether that's writing code, using a computer, or doing research, then what matters isn't whether the model can produce a beautiful video. It's whether it can anticipate the consequences of its own actions well enough to plan and correct itself. To me, that's the core of the concept: a world model is valuable to the extent that it lets you think before you act.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people use the same term but mean slightly different things.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "world model" is one of those terms that gets used in at least two or three different ways, and a lot of the confusion comes from people talking past each other.

The first sense is the narrow, almost engineering one. In reinforcement learning, a world model is just a learned transition function: given the current state and an action, predict the next state, maybe the reward. That's the Dyna tradition, that's Ha and Schmidhuber's "World Models" paper, that's MuZero. Here it's a very concrete object. You use it to plan, to simulate rollouts, to reduce how much you have to interact with the real environment. Nobody is making any philosophical claims. It's a model of the dynamics of a specific environment.

The second sense is the one Yann LeCun and others push, which is more of a research program. The idea is that an intelligent system should have some internal representation of how the world works, in a predictive sense, and that this should be learned mostly from observation rather than language, and that it should operate in an abstract latent space rather than predicting pixels. That's a claim about what the right architecture for intelligence is, and it's partly a reaction against language models. The implicit argument is that text is a thin, lossy shadow of the world, so a model trained only on text can't really have a world model.

Then there's a third sense, which is how people talk about LLMs. When someone says "does GPT have a world model," they usually mean something like: does it have internal structure that corresponds to the actual state of things, as opposed to just surface statistics of tokens? The Othello-GPT work is the canonical example. You train a model on move sequences and find it represents the board internally. So the model isn't just memorizing sequences, it's building a representation of the state that generates the sequences.

My own view is that these are all pointing at the same underlying question, which is: what is the thing being represented, and what is it good for? I'd define a world model functionally. It's whatever internal state lets you predict the consequences of actions well enough to act. Under that definition, whether it comes from pixels or from text is secondary. What matters is whether the representation supports counterfactual reasoning. Can you ask "what if I did this instead" and get a useful answer.

And I think this connects directly to agents, which is what I care about. In the ReAct line of work, the reason reasoning helps acting is that the reasoning trace is essentially the model simulating the world in language. "If I search for this, I'll probably get a page that says that, then I should look for this." That's a rollout. It's a crude world model expressed in natural language rather than in a latent vector. The interesting thing is that it's compositional and interpretable in a way that latent world models aren't, and it can borrow all of the model's prior knowledge.

So where I'd push back on the LeCun-style framing is that I don't think language is as impoverished as that view assumes. Humans wrote down an enormous amount of what they know about how the world works. The text corpus is a compressed world model already. The real gap, for me, isn't the modality. It's that language models learn from static data, so they've never experienced the consequences of their own actions. That's the piece a true world model needs, and that's why I think the next step is less about a new architecture and more about letting these models interact with environments and learn from feedback. The world model you get from being in the loop is different in kind from the one you get from reading about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says “world model” is used in at least two or three different ways and describes researchers talking past each other.

astra-6.text:
I think “world model” is a somewhat overloaded term. Different researchers use it to mean different things, so I’d first ask: what is the world you’re modeling, and what do you need that model to do?

In a relatively narrow sense, a world model predicts how an environment changes. Given the current state and an action, what happens next? That’s useful for planning: instead of trying every action in the real environment, an agent can imagine possible outcomes and choose what to do.

But people also use the term more broadly to mean an internal understanding of how the world works. In that sense, a language model might contain aspects of a world model, because predicting text requires learning something about the situations that text describes. The harder question is whether that understanding is reliable enough to support decisions, especially in unfamiliar situations.

I wouldn’t restrict the concept to predicting video or simulating physical environments. For an agent operating on a computer, the relevant world includes files, programs, and interfaces. Predicting what happens when you run a command is also a kind of world modeling.

So, to me, the useful question is less whether a system ‘has a world model’ as a yes-or-no property, and more: what can it predict, under which actions, and how well do those predictions help it accomplish a task?

r001.rationale: The candidate calls “world model” an overloaded term and says different researchers use it to mean different things.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “world model” is a fairly broad term, and different researchers use it to mean different things. My interpretation is that it’s an internal model that lets an agent predict how its environment will change, especially in response to its actions.

For example, if I move a cup toward the edge of a table, what happens next? A world model lets me anticipate the consequences without actually trying every possible action. That makes it useful for planning: you can imagine several futures, compare them, and decide what to do.

But the “world” doesn’t have to be the physical world. For an agent using a computer, it might mean predicting what clicking a button or running a command will do. And the model doesn’t necessarily have to generate images or video; it could represent those changes in language or some latent representation.

So I would distinguish between a model that can produce a plausible description of the world and a model that can reliably predict the consequences of actions. They overlap, but for building agents, I think the second capability is particularly important.

r001.rationale: The response says “different researchers use it to mean different things,” directly expressing the criterion.
